title: THE FORGOTTEN SON OF JONATHAN
paragraphs: Some stories do not begin with triumph.
In the silence after a funeral.
In the ruins left behind when everything familiar collapses.
Some stories begin with a little boy running for his life.
Very few remember the forgotten son.
Yet hidden within his story is one of the most breathtaking portraits of the Gospel in all of Scripture.
It is a story of tragedy, brokenness, covenant love, undeserved grace, restored identity, and a King who refuses to forget.
It is the story of every believer.
And perhaps, it is your story too.
The story begins during one of Israel's darkest moments.
King Saul and Jonathan had fallen in battle against the Philistines.
The news spread rapidly through the land.
In the ancient Near East, when a new dynasty rose to power, surviving descendants of the former king were often eliminated to prevent future claims to the throne.
Among those caught in the chaos was a five-year-old boy.

"Jonathan the son of Saul had a son who was crippled in his feet. He was five years old when the news about Saul and Jonathan came from Jezreel, and his nurse took him up and fled. And as she fled in her haste, he fell and became lame. And his name was Mephibosheth."
(2 Samuel 4:4)
One moment he was a prince.
The next moment he was broken.
Not because of anything he had done.
He was wounded because the world around him collapsed.
How many people know that feeling?
Yet somehow you still carry the limp.
Mephibosheth became the visible reminder of a kingdom that had fallen.
The son of Jonathan disappeared into obscurity.
Far from the life he was born to inherit.
Scripture says he lived in Lo-debar.
The Hebrew phrase לֹא דְבָר (Lo-Debar) carries the idea of barrenness, emptiness, and a place with no pasture.
It was the perfect picture of spiritual hopelessness.
But heaven specializes in finding forgotten people.
Years earlier, David and Jonathan had entered into a covenant.

"Jonathan made a covenant with David because he loved him as his own soul."
(1 Samuel 18:3)
Jonathan knew David would one day become king.
Yet he willingly surrendered his own claim.
His loyalty was not based upon personal gain.
Years later, after Jonathan's death, David remembered.
David remembered because covenant love never forgets.
Then comes one of the most beautiful questions in Scripture:

"Is there still anyone left of the house of Saul, that I may show him kindness for Jonathan's sake?"
(2 Samuel 9:1)
Everything that follows is based entirely upon covenant.
The Hebrew word translated "kindness" is חֶסֶד (chesed).
This is one of the richest words in the entire Old Testament.
David was not searching for someone worthy.
He was searching for someone covered by covenant.
Because the Gospel works the same way.
We are not saved because we are worthy.
We are saved because Jesus is worthy.
We are not accepted for our sake.
We are accepted for Christ's sake.
We are not invited because we earned favor.
We are invited because grace found us.
When David's servants located Mephibosheth, he was likely terrified.
A summons from the king usually meant judgment.
Especially for descendants of a former royal line.
The king knows where I am.
The king is calling for me.
Yet when Mephibosheth arrived before David, something unexpected happened.
And ultimately to sinners standing before a holy God.

"I will show you kindness for the sake of your father Jonathan, and I will restore to you all the land of Saul your father, and you shall eat at my table always."
(2 Samuel 9:7)
Everything changed in a single sentence.
The orphan found a seat at the King's table.
His response reveals how he saw himself:

"What is your servant, that you should show regard for a dead dog such as I?"
(2 Samuel 9:8)
Many people secretly speak to themselves that way.
Maybe not with those exact words.
But the message remains the same.
But grace does not consult your self-assessment.
The New Testament reveals that better word in Greek.
God's freely given kindness toward the undeserving.
The Gospel is not the story of good people climbing toward God.
It is the story of a gracious King descending toward broken people.
That is exactly what happened to Mephibosheth.
David adopted him into royal fellowship.
The initiative belonged entirely to the king.
Just as salvation belongs entirely to Christ.
Then Scripture records one of the most moving descriptions in the chapter:

"So Mephibosheth ate at David's table, like one of the king's sons."
(2 Samuel 9:11)
Every meal became a visible sermon.
Every seat at the table became a testimony.
Every gathering proclaimed the same truth.
Grace is greater than your limp.
There is another detail many overlook.
When Mephibosheth sat at the king's table, his crippled feet disappeared beneath the tablecloth.
The very thing that defined him no longer determined his place.
The king's provision covered his weakness.
The king's presence overshadowed his brokenness.
The king's acceptance rewrote his identity.
Yet our standing before God is not determined by our limp.
When the Father sees those who belong to Jesus, He sees them clothed in the righteousness of His Son.
The Apostle Paul would later write:
Because Jesus has already carried the judgment.
This is why the story of Mephibosheth continues to captivate hearts centuries later.
We were hiding in our own Lo-debar.
Unable to earn a place at the King's table.
Yet Jesus came looking for us.
The Son of David remembered His covenant.
The cross became the ultimate demonstration of God's חֶסֶד (chesed).
At Calvary, justice and mercy met.
Perhaps you have spent years believing your failures define you.
Perhaps shame has become your identity.
Perhaps you have convinced yourself that God has moved on without you.
The King still seats broken people at His table.
Because grace does not merely improve lives.
And that is exactly what Jesus does.
If this story stirred something deep inside you, do not keep it to yourself.
Which part of Mephibosheth's story felt most like your own? Was it the fall, the hiding, the fear, or the moment grace found him?

Supporting this work helps spread biblical truth, reach more hearts, and create more Scripture-rich content that points people to Christ. If your desire is to glorify God through the advancement of the Gospel, your partnership becomes part of that mission.
Because sometimes the greatest miracle is not that God removes the limp—but that He gives the limping a permanent seat at His table.
